newsitem.title: RUSSIA: S.Korean consul slain in Russia, big probe starts.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean consul slain in Russia, big probe starts.

text.p: A South Korean diplomat in Russia's crime-ridden Far East port of Vladivostok has been found bludgeoned to death outside his apartment, local police said on Wednesday.

"We are investigating the killing. Nobody has been arrested," a police spokesman told Reuters. He gave no further details about the killing, which took place on Tuesday evening as the diplomat, Choi Duck-keun, returned to his apartment.

Vladivostok, seven time zones ahead of Moscow and tucked between China and the Sea of Japan, has been dubbed Russia's "wild east" -- a final frontier of capitalism bedevilled by turf battles between rival mafia gangs.

District Prosecutor Oleg Logunov told Itar-Tass news agency that around 200 specialists from the police, the federal services and state prosecution had been drafted onto the Choi case, which would be headed by the region's 10 top detectives.
He said investigators would consider a range of motives for the attack, including personal vendetta, robbery and the possibility of a North Korean connection, Tass reported.
In Seoul, Foreign Ministry spokesman Suh Dae-won said Choi had been killed on the stairs of his apartment building by unidentified men.

"What we know officially from our investigations is that he was hit on the head by a very heavy tool," he said. His wallet, passport, cash and other personal belongings were untouched, but there was a cut around his midriff.

Suh declined all comment on South Korean media reports suggesting that North Korea was behind the killing, which took place amid rising tension between Seoul and Pyongyang and North Korean threats of retaliation over a submarine incident.
Tass said Logunov believed the involvement of Pyongyang in the killing was "improbable", though it added that several hundred North Korean construction workers lived in Vladivostok.

After his attackers had delivered their first blow, Choi had run up the stairs screaming for help. Neighbours found him lying unconscious on the floor and he died on the way to hospital, it quoted Logunov as saying.
A foreign ministry official said Moscow was assisting in bringing Choi's relatives to Vladivostok. A South Korean coroner may also come, Tass reported.

Korean state radio said South Korean diplomats had been warned to take extra precautions following a threat by North Korea to retaliate unless South Korea returned a submarine that intruded into the South two weeks ago.

Pyongyang has demanded the immediate return of the vessel along with its surviving and dead crew. The submarine landed an estimated 26 North Koreans, and of these 22 have been killed and one captured alive during a manhunt.
The domestic Yonhap news agency said Choi was in charge of North Korean affairs at the consulate.

Vladivostok, which is 9,200 km (5,700 miles) east of Moscow, was a closed naval city until 1990. A city of Soviet high-rise blocks and faded 19th century villas, it lies just 160 km (100 miles) from the North Korean and Chinese borders.
It has a small resident South Korean business community. China and Japan are also keen to boost commercial links with Vladivostok, whose name in Russian means ruler of the east.
The city, which has around 700,000 inhabitants, sees itself as an eastern San Francisco due to its hilly location overlooking the Pacific.
Contract killings, often involving car bombs, have become commonplace in recent years, spawned by a prevailing "anything goes" climate as free enterprise flourishes.
Choi was transferred to Vladivostok in 1995 from the consulate in Kiev, where his son now attends university. His wife was with him in Vladivostok. A daughter lives in Seoul.
